paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions before knowing future requests. This paper studies how predictions can help when their reliability is expressed as a probability of being correct. Its assumption is deliberately permissive: each prediction is correct with probability at least epsilon, while an incorrect prediction can be arbitrarily inaccurate.

The authors design algorithms for caching and covering problems under this prediction model. They establish an O(log(1/epsilon)) competitive guarantee for caching and an O(1/epsilon) guarantee for a broad family of covering problems, including set cover and facility location. These guarantees describe how an algorithm's cost compares with an optimal solution that knows the future.

The central finding is that even predictions with a small probability of correctness can substantially improve on worst-case bounds for these problems. The benefit does not require every prediction error to be small. Instead, the algorithms exploit the stated probability of receiving correct information, with guarantees that become weaker as that probability decreases.
neurips-2022-augmenting-online-algorithm.tldr: Predictions that are occasionally correct can improve online algorithms even when their other predictions are arbitrarily inaccurate.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label text classification requires selecting relevant labels from a collection that can contain millions of possibilities. A label tree organizes this enormous choice space into different resolutions. The paper examines how transformer-based classifiers represent text when making decisions across those resolutions, where computational demands and prediction quality both matter.

The authors identify a shortcoming in existing transformer approaches: they do not maintain separate feature representations for each resolution in the label tree. CascadeXML addresses this through an end-to-end training pipeline that uses the transformer's multiple layers to attend to different label resolutions. Each resolution can therefore use a separate representation within the same overall model.

The reported experiments show substantial improvements over existing approaches on benchmark datasets containing up to three million labels. These findings support matching the model's internal representations to the multiple resolutions of the classification problem. The contribution is a way to organize transformer learning around that structure while training the complete pipeline together.
neurips-2022-cascadexml-rethinking-trans.tldr: CascadeXML uses different transformer representations for different label-tree resolutions, improving classification on benchmarks with millions of labels.

paragraphs: Learning from time series can involve two distinct goals: classifying cause and effect, and preserving causal relationships when transforming the data into features. This paper investigates both using Neurochaos Learning, a brain-inspired learning algorithm. Its examples include coupled autoregressive processes, two kinds of coupled chaotic maps, and a real-world prey-predator system.

For classification with coupled skew tent maps, Neurochaos Learning consistently outperforms a five-layer deep neural network and an LSTM over unidirectional coupling coefficients from 0.1 to 0.7. The authors separately examine the extracted features using Granger Causality for autoregressive processes and Compression-Complexity Causality for the chaotic systems and prey-predator data.

In these investigations, Neurochaos Learning preserves the causal structure present in the input time series, unlike the tested deep neural network, LSTM, and one-dimensional convolutional network. This suggests that useful classification features can also retain information about causal relationships. The findings motivate exploring more sophisticated causal learning tasks, rather than establishing performance on those tasks already.
neurips-2022-causality-preserving-chaoti.tldr: Neurochaos Learning preserves causal structure in the studied time-series transformations and improves classification in a specified chaotic-system setting.

paragraphs: Text generators produce sequences one step at a time, making sequence-level training signals valuable. Contrastive learning offers such a signal by teaching a model to distinguish between examples. The paper investigates why earlier uses of contrastive learning for generation often performed poorly despite their potential to alleviate exposure bias.

CoNT addresses three parts of the generation pipeline together: how contrastive examples are constructed, which contrastive loss is used, and how decoding is performed. This scope matters because the proposed framework treats the training examples, learning objective, and generation procedure as connected sources of performance, rather than focusing on the objective alone.

Evaluation covers ten benchmarks across translation, summarization, code comment generation, data-to-text generation, and commonsense generation. CoNT improves over its baseline on all ten. Against the strongest previous contrastive method, the reported gains include 1.50 BLEU for translation and 1.77 ROUGE-1 for summarization. It also achieves reported state-of-the-art results in summarization, code comments without external data, and data-to-text generation.
neurips-2022-cont-contrastive-neural-tex.tldr: CoNT improves text generation by jointly addressing contrastive example construction, training loss, and decoding.

paragraphs: Logic gates such as AND and XOR perform simple operations that can execute very quickly. This paper explores learning networks made from combinations of these gates for machine learning tasks. The attraction is efficient prediction, but conventional logic gates create a training problem: their discrete behavior does not directly support gradient descent.

The proposed architecture makes the learning process differentiable by combining real-valued logic with a continuously parameterized relaxation of the network. This gives training a smooth version of the gate choices to work with. The resulting network is then discretized, allowing prediction to use the logic-gate form whose execution speed motivated the approach.

The authors report inference speeds exceeding one million MNIST images per second on a single CPU core. This illustrates the efficiency achievable with the resulting discretized networks in that task. The contribution connects a trainable continuous representation with fast discrete computation, making combinations of logic gates accessible to gradient-based learning.
neurips-2022-deep-differentiable-logic-g.tldr: A differentiable relaxation lets logic-gate networks train with gradients and then execute rapidly as discrete networks.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional object detectors often combine information from multiple modalities to improve their predictions. This paper argues that existing fusion strategies can overlook useful information specific to each modality. Combining inputs is therefore only part of the challenge: the detector also needs to retain the distinctive information each input provides.

DeepInteraction learns and maintains a separate representation for each modality throughout detection. Those representations interact through an architecture with two main components: an encoder for interaction between multimodal representations and a decoder for interaction during prediction. The design allows information to pass between modalities while preserving representations in which their individual characteristics remain available.

Experiments on nuScenes show that DeepInteraction surpasses prior methods, often by a large margin, and the paper reports first place on its object detection leaderboard. These results support modality interaction as an effective design for the evaluated detection setting. The broader architectural lesson is that maintaining distinct representations can matter alongside enabling information exchange between them.
neurips-2022-deepinteraction-3d-object-d.tldr: DeepInteraction improves 3D detection by letting modalities exchange information while maintaining their separate representations.

paragraphs: A language model can learn a new task from a few examples placed directly in its input, without gradient-based training. However, this in-context approach processes the examples again for every prediction, creating repeated computation, memory, and storage costs. The paper compares it with parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which trains a small collection of parameters for the task.

The authors introduce (IA)^3, a method that scales model activations using learned vectors. It adds relatively few parameters while delivering stronger performance in their comparison. They also develop T-Few, a recipe based on T0 that can be applied to new tasks without task-specific changes or tuning.

The experiments find that few-shot parameter-efficient fine-tuning achieves better accuracy with dramatically lower computational costs than in-context learning. On completely unseen RAFT tasks, T-Few exceeds the human-performance reference and improves on the previous state of the art by six percentage points. These results show the practical value of learning a small adaptation instead of repeatedly supplying demonstrations at prediction time.
neurips-2022-few-shot-parameter-efficien.tldr: Few-shot parameter-efficient fine-tuning outperforms in-context learning in the reported comparison while substantially reducing computational costs.

paragraphs: Paraphrase identification asks whether two pieces of text express the same meaning. Strong models can lose accuracy when the examples encountered during use differ from their training distribution. This paper identifies biases introduced by negative examples, pairs that are not paraphrases, as a major contributor to that performance drop.

GAPX separates the learning process into two models: one trained only on positive pairs and another trained only on negative pairs. This separation makes the influence of negative examples adjustable at prediction time. The authors introduce a perplexity-based measure of distribution shift that automatically determines how much weight to give the negative model.

The reported empirical results support both the diagnosis of negative-example bias and the proposed response. The approach matters because information learned from non-paraphrases need not have the same usefulness across different input distributions. Giving that information a separately controlled contribution lets the system adapt its reliance on it when making predictions on unfamiliar data.
neurips-2022-gapx-generalized-autoregres.tldr: GAPX addresses distribution shift in paraphrase identification by separately learning from negative pairs and adapting their influence at inference.

paragraphs: A graph prediction model may encounter test data drawn from a different distribution than its training data. GOOD provides a systematic benchmark for studying this problem. It covers both predictions about entire graphs and predictions about individual nodes, recognizing that constructing meaningful distribution shifts differs between these two tasks.

The benchmark explicitly separates covariate shifts from concept shifts and includes settings with no shift. It combines 11 datasets and 17 domain selections into 51 data splits. The authors evaluate ten commonly used baseline methods with ten random runs, covering 510 dataset-model combinations. This structure allows performance to be compared across distinct kinds of change.

The results reveal substantial gaps between performance within the training distribution and performance outside it. They also show that methods have different performance trends under covariate and concept shifts. These findings make the kind of shift an important part of evaluation: success under one setting does not summarize a method's behavior across the benchmark's other settings.
neurips-2022-good-a-graph-out-of-distrib.tldr: GOOD systematically evaluates graph prediction under different distribution shifts and reveals substantial generalization gaps.

paragraphs: Neural rendering can reconstruct shapes without direct 3D supervision, but the resulting surfaces often lose fine geometric detail. HF-NeuS addresses this oversmoothing using a signed distance function, a representation that describes a surface through distances to it. The method targets both how this representation connects to rendering and how it is optimized.

The authors analyze the relationships between the signed distance function, density, transparency, and rendering weights, then model transparency through a transformed signed distance function. They also identify unstable optimization when one function must learn coarse structure and fine detail together. Their solution separates base geometry from displacement and gradually introduces higher-frequency detail through coarse-to-fine learning.

An adaptive optimization strategy further concentrates training on regions near the surface where artifacts remain. Together, these choices organize learning around increasingly detailed geometry and targeted corrections. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations show finer reconstructed surface details and better reconstruction quality than the state-of-the-art methods considered in the paper.
neurips-2022-hf-neus-improved-surface-re.tldr: HF-NeuS reconstructs finer surfaces by separating coarse geometry from detail and concentrating optimization near surface artifacts.

paragraphs: Advertising incrementality measures the causal effect of showing an advertisement compared with not showing it. This paper asks how an advertiser can learn a sequence of bids without knowing those effects beforehand. The learning problem is complicated because feedback about additional conversions arrives late and combines contributions rather than presenting a straightforward immediate reward.

The authors first express the offline problem as an episodic Markov decision process with special structure. They then develop a reinforcement learning algorithm for its online counterpart. To learn conversion incrementality from the mixed and delayed observations, they introduce and analyze a pairwise moment-matching algorithm as a central component.

The resulting regret guarantee is at most O-tilde(H squared times the square root of T), where H counts rounds and T counts episodes. The bound does not depend on the number of possible bids. This theoretical result shows how the problem's structure can support learning despite difficult reward feedback, without adding a dependence on action count to the stated guarantee.
neurips-2022-incrementality-bidding-via-.tldr: A reinforcement learning approach learns incrementality-based bidding from mixed, delayed rewards with a regret bound independent of the number of bids.

paragraphs: Kernel similarity matching seeks representations whose similarities reflect kernel-based similarities between inputs. Earlier neural approaches applied linear similarity matching to nonlinear features generated using random Fourier methods. This paper instead learns the nonlinear features directly, connecting representation learning with online rules based on correlations between neural activities.

The method derives and minimizes an upper bound on the total squared error between input kernel similarities and output similarities. The form of this bound produces learning rules that can be implemented in a single-layer recurrent neural network. It also naturally produces sparse representations that respond selectively to particular input patterns, alongside high-dimensional representations that are linearly separable.

The authors compare approximation quality with neural random Fourier features and variants of the Nyström method. Their approach appears comparable to or better than randomly sampled Nyström methods when output representations are relatively low dimensional, even if larger than the inputs. At very high output dimensions, its approximations are less faithful, making output dimensionality a meaningful qualification of the reported comparison.
neurips-2022-kernel-similarity-matching-.tldr: A recurrent network learns nonlinear kernel features through correlation-based updates, with approximation quality that depends on output dimensionality.

paragraphs: Simulating a system governed by partial differential equations can require repeatedly updating many small spatial cells. That makes following large systems over time computationally expensive. This paper introduces LE-PDE, which learns a compact representation of the whole system and advances that representation through time.

The central idea is to perform the evolving computation entirely in a learned latent space: a smaller set of variables representing the system. Updating fewer variables can reduce the work required over a long sequence of simulation steps. The authors also introduce training objectives designed to keep these learned dynamics stable over long simulations, addressing the need for useful predictions beyond a short time horizon.

The method also tackles inverse optimization of boundary conditions, where the task is to adjust those conditions to obtain a desired flow behavior. It computes updates by backpropagating through the sequence of latent states. An additional annealing technique addresses boundary conditions that are non-differentiable and interact sparsely with the system.

The authors test LE-PDE on one-dimensional nonlinear equations, two-dimensional Navier–Stokes flows reaching turbulence, and a boundary-condition optimization problem. Against leading learned simulators and other strong comparisons, they report up to 128-fold fewer dimensions to update and up to 15-fold faster computation, with competitive accuracy. These reported gains show that compact global evolution can substantially accelerate the tested tasks while retaining useful predictive accuracy.
neurips-2022-learning-to-accelerate-part.tldr: LE-PDE accelerates PDE simulation and boundary-condition optimization by evolving a compact global representation, reporting up to 15-fold faster computation with competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: Training an image-generating adversarial network with limited data can lead to trivial solutions and training failures. MaskedGAN addresses this by randomly hiding some image information during training. The purpose is to make learning from the available images more demanding and encourage attention to the image as a whole.

The method combines two complementary masking strategies. Shifted spatial masking removes information across spatial dimensions with random shifts. Balanced spectral masking removes selected spectral bands using probabilities that adapt during training. Because the strategies act on different dimensions of image information, their combination provides a broader learning challenge than either type of masking alone.

The experiments report consistently superior performance across the tested architectures and datasets. These include convolutional models such as BigGAN and StyleGAN-v2, transformer models such as TransGAN and GANformer, and datasets ranging from CIFAR and ImageNet to faces and street scenes. The results support masking as a broadly applicable training intervention for the limited-data generation settings examined.
neurips-2022-masked-generative-adversari.tldr: MaskedGAN improves image generation with limited data by combining spatial and spectral masking during adversarial training.

paragraphs: When a decision problem offers an enormous number of options, observing every option even once may be too expensive. This paper studies pure exploration in stochastic multi-armed bandits when a graph describes similarities among the options. Its model assumes that rewards can be represented as a smooth signal on that graph.

The authors consider two goals: finding the option with the greatest reward and finding one whose reward is sufficiently high. They introduce GRUB and zeta-GRUB for these maximizing and satisficing problems. Their theoretical analysis explicitly characterizes the benefit of graph information, showing how relationships among options can help guide exploration.

A lower bound on required data identifies a large class of problems where the algorithms are near-optimal. Experiments also demonstrate benefits from using the graph. The important qualification is that the graph is paired with the reward-smoothness model: its value comes from providing relevant structure about the rewards, allowing exploration to use more than isolated observations of individual options.
neurips-2022-maximizing-and-satisficing-.tldr: GRUB and zeta-GRUB use graph relationships and reward smoothness to efficiently find the best or a sufficiently rewarding option.

paragraphs: Detecting three-dimensional objects from a single camera is difficult when the camera moves and objects appear at different distances. MoGDE uses the observation that an object's depth can be inferred from the ground where it stands. It repeatedly estimates ground depth and uses that information to guide object detection.

A pose detection network first estimates the camera's pose. Perspective geometry then produces a feature map describing ground depth at the pixel level. A transformer-based fusion network combines this estimated depth with image features. Its long-range attention helps identify ground-contact points and associate their ground depth with the relevant image information.

Experiments on KITTI show improvements in detection accuracy and robustness for both nearby and distant objects. The paper reports a large advantage over state-of-the-art methods and first place on the KITTI 3D benchmark. The approach makes ground contact a useful geometric reference for mobile monocular detection, linking camera pose estimation, depth construction, and visual features within one framework.
neurips-2022-mogde-boosting-mobile-monoc.tldr: MoGDE improves monocular 3D detection by estimating ground depth from camera pose and attaching it to object image features.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards are easier to specify than detailed reward functions, but they leave reinforcement learning agents with little guidance about where to explore. Demonstrations can provide an initial signal about promising behavior. This paper seeks a simple way to use that signal without the complexity and numerous hyperparameters of earlier demonstration-based methods.

Monte Carlo Actor-Critic initializes the replay buffer with demonstrations and changes the value-learning target. It takes the larger of the standard TD target and a Monte Carlo estimate of remaining reward. This encourages high estimated values around successful trajectories, giving the agent an incentive to explore their neighborhoods. The modification adds no tuning parameters.

Experiments across five continuous-control domains suggest that MCAC can substantially improve learning efficiency when applied to six existing reinforcement learning and demonstration-based algorithms. The contribution is a small change to standard actor-critic learning that makes demonstration returns influential during exploration, including in the setting of suboptimal demonstrations addressed by the paper.
neurips-2022-monte-carlo-augmented-actor.tldr: MCAC uses demonstration returns to raise value targets near successful trajectories, improving sparse-reward learning efficiency in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Graph smoothing repeatedly replaces a node's features with an average of its neighbors' features. Some averaging can help learning, but excessive averaging removes useful distinctions. On connected graphs, repeated mean aggregation eventually makes features constant across the graph. This paper develops an analysis that captures both the initial benefit and the later loss.

The authors study simplified linear graph neural networks under a latent-space random graph model. Node features reveal only part of the underlying latent variables, while graph edges provide pairwise information about them. In two examples, a finite number of averaging steps provably improves learning by recovering some of the information missing from the features.

The analysis identifies different mechanisms for regression and classification. For regression, less important directions shrink faster than principal directions. For classification, nodes within communities become similar faster than the communities collapse together. These results explain why an intermediate amount of smoothing helps in the studied models, while continuing the same operation eventually destroys that advantage.
neurips-2022-not-too-little-not-too-much.tldr: The analysis proves how finite graph smoothing can improve learning in two models before excessive averaging erases useful distinctions.

paragraphs: Personalized models use attributes such as age group or sex with the expectation that disclosure improves predictions. This paper asks when the available data can establish that every participating group benefits. It introduces the benefit of personalization, or BoP, as the smallest accuracy improvement expected by any group.

The authors use BoP to construct hypothesis tests for improvement across all groups and procedures that bound the minimum improvement. They analyze the reliability of both with finite datasets, deriving minimax bounds on testing error and estimation error. The focus is what can be reliably verified about personalization, beyond whether a model improves accuracy on average.

Their results show that verifying a benefit for every group requires explicitly limiting the number of group attributes. In particular, reliable verification is impossible for a personalized classifier with at least 19 binary group attributes using eight billion samples. This does not establish that personalization harms a group; it establishes a severe limit on reliably confirming that every group gains.
neurips-2022-on-the-epistemic-limits-of-.tldr: The paper establishes severe data limits on reliably verifying that personalization improves accuracy for every group.

paragraphs: In a sparse linear bandit, an agent repeatedly selects an action and observes a reward that depends linearly on only a few action features. Learning which features matter is therefore closely connected to choosing useful actions. This paper develops an estimator and an experimental-design criterion that address these two parts together.

The estimator, PopArt, has a tighter l1 recovery guarantee than Lasso, bounding the total absolute error in the recovered coefficients more tightly. Its bound motivates a convex experimental-design problem, making that design criterion computationally efficient to solve. The authors combine the estimator and design into algorithms for sequential action selection.

The resulting algorithms have improved regret upper bounds, particularly in how those bounds reflect the geometry of the available action set. The paper also proves a matching lower bound in the data-poor regime, closing a gap left by earlier bounds. This establishes a theoretical connection between better sparse estimation, effective data collection, and achievable decision-making performance.
neurips-2022-popart-efficient-sparse-reg.tldr: PopArt combines tighter sparse estimation guarantees with efficient experimental design to improve sparse linear bandit regret bounds.

paragraphs: Infomin learning aims to retain useful information in a representation while removing information about a specified target. Examples include reducing information about protected attributes or separating factors in learned representations. The usual objective involves mutual information, which measures dependence between the representation and the information the learner is meant to discard.

Existing approaches often train an additional neural network to estimate mutual information or a substitute for it. This adversarial procedure can be slow and difficult to optimize. The authors use slicing techniques to construct a new proxy for mutual information, then derive an accurate approximation that can be computed analytically. This removes the need for a neural mutual-information estimator.

Experiments cover algorithmic fairness, disentangled representation learning, and domain adaptation. Within a limited time budget, the proposed method removes unwanted information more effectively than the evaluated baselines. The findings support simplifying the dependence-measurement component of infomin learning so that more effective information removal can be achieved within practical computational constraints.
neurips-2022-scalable-infomin-learning-3.tldr: An analytically computable mutual-information proxy makes unwanted-information removal more effective within the tested time budgets.

paragraphs: Neural networks initialized with small weights can exhibit condensation: hidden neurons' input weights, including their biases, gather around a limited number of directions. When many neurons align this way, the network behaves as though it has a smaller effective size. This paper studies how that organization forms at the beginning of training.

The authors examine multilayer fully connected networks and connect the maximum number of condensed directions to the activation function's multiplicity at zero, meaning its root multiplicity there. They show that the maximum number is twice this multiplicity. This links an aspect of early network organization to a mathematical property of the activation.

The theoretical analysis confirms experiments in two settings: multiplicity-one activations with inputs of arbitrary dimension, and layers with one-dimensional inputs and arbitrary activation multiplicity. These specified cases provide a step toward explaining how small initialization induces early condensation. The result concerns the initial training stage and helps clarify one mechanism through which training can implicitly favor a smaller effective network.
neurips-2022-towards-understanding-the-c.tldr: The paper connects early neural-network weight condensation under small initialization to the activation function's root multiplicity at zero.

paragraphs: Motion can reveal object boundaries in video, but an object does not stop existing when it stops moving. This paper uses that observation to learn multi-object segmentation without manual labels. Video provides the training supervision, while the learned model can separate objects in a single still image.

The model predicts regions that could exhibit motion characteristic of rigid objects. Instead of assigning one specific motion to a region, it predicts a distribution of possible motions, including no movement. This accounts for the ambiguity of a still image and allows motion-based supervision to support recognizing objects that are stationary.

Experiments show advantages over a deterministic version and report state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation on simulated and real-world benchmarks. The method also surpasses approaches that receive motion information at test time. Applying the approach to existing image-reconstruction models yields large improvements, supporting its usefulness across different segmentation architectures. The central contribution is treating motion as a range of object-compatible possibilities during learning.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-multi-object-s.tldr: Learning distributions of possible object motions from video enables unsupervised segmentation of multiple objects in still images.

paragraphs: Vertical federated learning trains models using data whose different features are held by different participants. Adding participants can create scalability problems without a corresponding improvement in model quality. This paper asks how to identify a small, important subset of participants before committing to training with the full consortium.

The authors formulate participant selection through mutual information and introduce VF-MINE, an estimator designed for vertically federated data. It uses Fagin's algorithm from database theory as a building block. Further optimization produces VF-PS, a participant-selection framework based on group testing. Together, these components provide a way to assess informative participation without first training the complete federated model.

Empirical results show that participant selection can run orders of magnitude faster than full VFL training. The selected participants often support a model of similar quality to one using the larger group. The qualification matters: comparable quality is an observed frequent outcome, while the practical contribution is making selective participation computationally attractive in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-vf-ps-how-to-select-importa.tldr: VF-PS efficiently selects informative vertical-federated-learning participants, often retaining similar model quality with a smaller group.

paragraphs: A model's behavior on training data may differ sharply from its behavior on unseen data, including in robustness and subgroup performance. This paper formalizes the desirable correspondence between those behaviors through distributional generalization. The authors call it a What You See Is What You Get property and show that differentially private training provably provides it.

The connection gives a design principle: within the established framework, mitigating unwanted behavior on training data is sufficient to mitigate it at test time. This turns a generalization concern into an optimization problem. The principle is a sufficiency result tied to the paper's differential-privacy connection, rather than a claim that arbitrary training procedures transfer every observed behavior.

Using this principle, the authors construct simple methods competitive with leading approaches in several distributional-robustness applications. They also improve the privacy-versus-disparate-impact trade-off of DP-SGD and reduce robust overfitting in adversarial training. Additional theoretical results tighten relationships among differential privacy, stability, and distributional generalization, supporting both the conceptual framework and its applications.
neurips-2022-what-you-see-is-what-you-ge.tldr: Differentially private training provides a distributional-generalization principle for translating improvements in training behavior into improvements at test time.
